newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen says may drop Cambodia's ASEAN bid.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen says may drop Cambodia's ASEAN bid.

text.p: Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said on Monday Cambodia might withdraw its application to join ASEAN if the group continued to interfere in the country's internal affairs.

The Association of South East Asian Nations said last week it was postponing Cambodia's membership in the grouping, originally scheduled for later this month, in response to Hun Sen's violent ouster last week of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
"We consider if we go to ASEAN or if we stop. I want to stop if ASEAN continues to interfere in our internal affairs," Hun Sen told reporters at a pagoda opening in this province north of Phnom Penh.
"I am afraid of joining ASEAN because of ASEAN interference in internal affairs," he said. He said he was discussing the matter with his senior ministers.
ASEAN said last week it still recognised Ranariddh as first prime minister, and said it would try to work out a ceasefire between forces loyal to the rival Cambodian premiers.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

It said last week that it would send envoys to talk to Ranariddh, Hun Sen and King Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing, where the monarch is receiving medical treatment, in an effort to find a solution to the crisis.
Hun Sen warned major powers not to use aid as a tool to threaten him and said no country should interfere in Cambodia's internal affairs.

"You cannot come and say 'Excellency, you must do this or do that because my country has helped you a lot'," he said. "Business is different from aid. You should not want to threaten Hun Sen, you can threaten anyone else, that's all right, but not Hun Sen."

The United States said last week it was suspending its aid to Cambodia for 30 days in response to the violent overthrow of Ranariddh on July 6. Ranariddh left the country two days before his overthrow.
Germany suspended its aid programme indefinitely and Australia said it was considering suspending its assistance to Cambodia.
"No foreigner, no powerful country, can threaten Hun Sen. The only people who have the right to control Hun Sen are the Cambodian people," Hun Sen said.

Hun Sen also said on Monday that the United Nations, and France and Indonesia, co-chairs of the 1991 Paris peace agreement that paved the way for Cambodia's U.N.-organised elections in 1993, should ignore Ranariddh.

"The U.N. Security Council and the co-chairman of the Paris peace agreement please end the affair of Norodom Ranariddh and let us finish this matter by way of the courts and through FUNCINPEC sovereignty," he said, referring to Ranariddh's royalist party.
Hun Sen has told members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party remaining in Cambodia to choose a new first prime minister. He has said he does not want to become first prime minister.

Hun Sen said Ranariddh should be prosecuted for illegal negotiations with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and his alleged illegal import of weapons. On Monday he said he was taking steps to have the prince brought back for trial and asking Cambodian legal authorities to prepare an international warrant for his arrest.

On Sunday Hun Sen said in a radio broadcast that Cambodia must have a free and fair election. He did not give a date for the poll but he and Ranariddh agreed last month that the election should be on May 23.
